h: פָּרָשַׁת פָּרָה, מַאֲמָר ה׳ Parshas Parah — Maamar Hei

p: בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (מְגִילָּה פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ה כה, ב)
"We do not interrupt between Parah and HaChodesh.
The sign for these parshiyos is
if he wishes to drink, he may drink;
between the third and the fourth he may not drink.'"
And certainly the words of the Yerushalmi
are not said merely as a mnemonic sign,
the matter of reading the four parshiyos
which correspond to the four expressions
Now, "I will take out," "I will rescue," and "I will redeem" —
all of them signify going out from evil,
and they allude to the purification of the soul
from the three kelipos of impurity:
which remove a person from the world
And they are the three kinds of impurity of the soul:
the metzora, the zav, and one impure through a corpse.
For tzaraas is anger and jealousy,
for which he is sent out
even from the camp of Yisrael,
has no root at all in holiness.
And for this the rectification comes
shall owe a beka per head,
(and so it is in Tanchuma Ki Sisa 10
וּבִירוּשַׁלְמִי שְׁקָלִים פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ג ט, ב)
And the sale of Yosef came from jealousy,
And the zav, which comes from desire,
is sent out only from the Levite camp,
because it has a root in holiness —
for this the yetzer was created,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כט, יח]
along the lines of what is said (I Divrei HaYamim 29:18),
"the inclination of the thoughts of the heart of Your people."
It is only you who make it bad
(as is written in Midrash Tanchuma Bereishis 7).
And in any case, into the Levite camp,
so that he will be free for Torah —
כִּי הַתּוֹרָה הוּא תַּבְלִין לְיֵצֶר הָרָע
for the Torah is the antidote to the yetzer hara,
meaning the yetzer hara of desire —
וְעַל זֶה בָּא קְרִיאַת פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר
And for this comes the reading of Parshas Zachor,
to wipe out the memory of Amalek
and it is stated (Midrash Tanchuma Ki Seitzei 9):
אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִהְיֶה טָהוֹר מִקְּרֵה לָיְלָה,
'who will not be pure from a nocturnal occurrence';
and also that he would hurl the circumcised members
for this comes through the counsel of the serpent,
who brought death to the world
by what he put into their hearts:
And this is the main root
of the primordial kings who died
the unfolding of the tzimtzum of creation,
which was in a garment of exaltation,
for there is no king without a people,
"Hashem reigns, He is clothed in majesty."
And this one is sent out
only from the camp of the Shechinah,
as we heard from our holy Rebbe,
זֵכֶר צַדִּיק וְקָדוֹשׁ לִבְרָכָה לְחַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
of blessed and holy memory, for the life of the World to Come,
on the verse, "And he was king in Yeshurun
when the heads of the people gathered" (Devarim 33:5) —
that only Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
compared to all the heads of the people,
"And the man Moshe was very humble," etc.
And this is why it says that he was king
And from arrogance there also branches out
when he feels lacking relative to his level,
and it is alluded to in the verse (Chavakuk 2:5),
כָּל אָדָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ גַּסּוּת הָרוּחַ
"Any person who has haughtiness of spirit,
his dust will not be stirred," etc.
that the Gemara's intent is not
that he will not rise at the resurrection of the dead at all,
for if so, you have left no life
Rather, the intent of "his dust will not be stirred"
is that he will not rise in his dust
like one who wakes from his sleep,
you who dwell in the dust" —
one who made himself a neighbor to dust during his life;
such a one will be like one waking from his sleep.
which is why death is called,
"'When you lie down, it will guard you' (Mishlei 6:22) —
'and when you awaken, it will converse with you' (ibid.) —
"The long and short days have come;
אֲבָל אֵין כַּוָּנַת חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה
שֶׁמִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִטְהַר נַפְשׁוֹ מִזֶּה בְּתַכְלִית
that one whose soul is not completely purified of this
לֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ תְּקוּמָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
will have no rising, Heaven forbid.
וְעַל זֶה מְרַמֵּז קְרִיאַת פָּרָשַׁת פָּרָה
And to this the reading of Parshas Parah alludes:
to the ultimate purification of the soul,
even from the aspect of impurity of the dead,
And to this the purification of the parah alludes,
which alludes to lowliness of the soul
And with this are completed and included
all three purifications of the soul before it,
and through this they become immediately prepared
for the resting of holiness in the soul
which corresponds to the fourth cup
which is the words of Torah and holiness
"the heart of the wise is at his right" —
פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ג יד, ב)
as it is written (Vayikra 16:19), 'And he shall purify it and sanctify it.'"
And this is what they said in the sign:
"between the third and the fourth he may not drink" —
that we do not interrupt between Parah and HaChodesh,
for Parah corresponds to "I will redeem,"
which is the completion of the redemption from evil,
And HaChodesh corresponds to "I will take,"
which is the words of Torah and holiness,
and they are contiguous: "he shall purify it and sanctify it."

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 3:5 — “Rabbi Levi said in Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's name: One does not interrupt between Parah and HaChodesh. Rabbi Levi said: Their mnemonic is the cups: between these cups, if one wishes to drink, he may drink; between the third and fourth he may not drink.” Rav Tzadok treats the mnemonic as reflecting an inward correspondence between the four readings and four cups.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Pesachim 10:7 — “They pour him a third cup, over which he recites the blessing for his food. Over the fourth he completes Hallel and recites the blessing of song. Between these cups, if he wishes to drink, he may drink; between the third and fourth he may not drink.”

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 88:5 — “Rav Huna said in Rabbi Benaya's name: The four cups correspond to the four redemptions stated concerning Egypt: I shall bring out, I shall rescue, I shall redeem, and I shall take. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said: They correspond to the four cups mentioned here in the chief cupbearer's account. Rabbi Levi said: They correspond to the four kingdoms.” The Midrash preserves several correspondences. Rav Tzadok follows the four expressions of redemption in explaining the sequence of purification.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avot 4:21 — “Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: Jealousy, desire, and honor remove a person from the world.” Rav Tzadok maps these three root traits onto the three forms of impurity and the purifying work of the readings.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 84:18 — “Rabbi Yehudah bar Simon said: The Holy One, blessed be He, told the tribes: You sold Rachel's son for twenty silver pieces; therefore each one's share shall be a beka per head, as it is written, A beka per head, half a shekel.” The Midrash relates the communal half-shekel to Yosef's sale. Rav Tzadok identifies jealousy as the fault rectified through Shekalim.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pekudei 6 — “Of the kelipah of jealousy nothing will remain, but of the yetzer of desire there will remain in the future a longing for Torah.” Rav Tzadok there cites Zohar I 138a: were it not for the yetzer, there would be no joy in learning. This is the source for the zav’s root in holiness, and it explains why desire is kept out only of the camp of the Levi’im.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Bereshit 7 — “If you say: Why did He create the evil inclination, of which it is written, The inclination of a person's heart is evil from his youth? You call it evil: who can make it good? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: You make it evil. ... How many things in the world are harsher and more bitter than the evil inclination, yet you sweeten them! Nothing is more bitter than lupines, yet you labor to cook and sweeten them in water seven times, until they become sweet. ... If you sweeten the bitter things I created for your needs, how much more the evil inclination, which is placed in your hands.” The source argues that the inclination can be transformed through effort. Rav Tzadok distinguishes redirecting desire toward holiness from traits that must be wholly uprooted.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Teitzei 9 — “Who encountered you: Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi Nechemyah, and the Sages disagreed. Rabbi Yehudah says: Encountered you means made you impure, as in One who is not pure through an occurrence by night. Rabbi Nechemyah says: He literally called you. ... The Sages say: Encountered you means cooled you before others.” Rav Tzadok follows Rabbi Yehudah's interpretation in linking Amalek with the impurity of a nocturnal emission; the Midrash also preserves other explanations.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Chanah Ariel (R' Aharon of Staroselye), Vayechi 2 — “There is no king without a people… so the earlier kings each said ‘I will reign’: to bring worlds into being as separate things, so that his kingship be called over them.” This develops Rav Tzadok’s point in Kabbalistic terms. The self-assertion that shattered the first kings is built into creation itself, since kingship needs others to rule over.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 47b — “The Master said: One who is arrogant is not accepted even by the members of his household, as it is said, An arrogant man shall not dwell at ease: not even in his own dwelling.” Rav Tzadok links the proud person's lack of inward repose with the sadness that follows frustrated self-importance.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 5a — “Rabbi Elazar said: Any person who possesses haughtiness of spirit, his dust is not awakened, as it is written, Awaken and sing, dwellers in dust. It does not say Those lying in dust, but Dwellers in dust: one who became a neighbor to the dust during his lifetime.” Rav Tzadok reads the wording as distinguishing effortless awakening from death, rather than denying every future restoration to anyone with an unrectified trace of pride.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Sotah 5a, s.v. Kol adam — “It is difficult: Why did the Mishnah of Chelek not count this? We also find in the final chapter of Kesubos that the dead outside the Land do not live, that the ignorant do not live unless they benefit Torah scholars, and in Aggadah that those who lend with interest do not live in the World to Come.” Tosafos raises the comparison to the Mishnah's list; the quoted comment does not provide Rav Tzadok's proposed resolution.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 65a — “Rav Chisda's daughter told him: Does the Master not wish to sleep a little? He answered: Now will come days that are long and short, and we shall sleep much.” The Gemara records Rav Chisda's response to the suggestion that he rest from study. Rav Tzadok adduces its idiom for the sleep of death.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Nasso 3 — on the metzora, zav and tamei lanefesh as jealousy, desire and honor: “So that a person not lose heart, each knowing the plagues of his own heart… the Torah teaches that for everything there is a repair.” There too the same reassurance follows the same three impurities. No blemish of the heart cuts a Jew off from Knesses Yisrael.
